bull_bear.body:
- Total borrowings cut to **Rs 1,500 cr** from Rs 1,699 cr YoY; cost of debt 7.42% (−115 bps); Debt/EBITDA ~2.25x.
- Post-demerger **Lemon Tree = zero-debt, cash-accretive**, no significant capex need → Board to set dividend / buyback / distribution policy; will "move into distribution of profit to shareholders." Very high hurdle rate for any acquisition (no F&B foray planned).
- **Fleur = capital-growth focused, not a dividend payer** currently — redeploys capital to grow inventory (Warburg backing).
bull_bear.title: Capital Allocation (net debt focus)

bull_bear.body:
- **Macro/geopolitical:** US–Iran war hitting discretionary/corporate travel (worst March–April; May "surprisingly good"); concern over oil/inflation/CAD spillover to Indian economy.
- **Aviation:** IndiGo Dec shutdown + both major carriers cutting metro-to-metro capacity for 3 months → demand/occupancy risk, esp. airport-market hotels (Aurika Mumbai).
- **Corporate-demand softness** (negotiated room nights 55% vs 59% YoY in Q4; full-year 55.4% vs 56.1% — modest); retail partly compensating at lower rates.
- **Sign-to-open slippage:** openings can slip 6+ months (never open early); owner financing risk on managed hotels.
- **Demerger timeline:** dependent on SEBI/shareholder/creditor approvals + NCLT (6–18 months variable). CCI approval received April.
- **Margin/incentive-fee sensitivity** to owned-hotel EBITDA delivery during renovation drag.
- **Supply glut** in specific micro-markets (e.g. ~2,000 keys added near Aurika Mumbai — Accor Fairmont, Novotel, Radisson, etc.).
bull_bear.title: Risks

bull_bear.body: Confident on structural India hospitality demand/supply gap and the demerger value-unlock; candid and granular on near-term war/aviation softness and on the deliberate margin sacrifice for catch-up renovation. Repeatedly **declined to give hard guidance** (fee/RevPAR/margin), preferring directional framing. Notable transparency: Keswani publicly corrected himself on the call re: Lemon Tree steady-state ~60% PAT margin. Leadership transition flagged — Keswani to become non-Executive Chair of LTH from March 2027, focusing on Fleur as Executive Chair.
bull_bear.title: Management Tone

bull_bear.body:
- Incentive fees scale 1%→5% of revenue by GOP/hotel-EBITDA slab — so owned-hotel renovation drag *mechanically* suppressed Fleur fee growth (8%) vs 3rd-party (23%); a self-reversing headwind as EBITDA recovers.
- Aurika Mumbai occupancy −2% driven by an ~8%-of-occupancy **wet-lease (airline crew) block going away**, replaced by ~6% higher-rated demand → net rate accretive (segment mix shift); company deliberately diversifying away from airline crew dependence.
- GST change (sub-Rs 7,500 room rate) is self-healing: as ARR/price hikes push more guests above Rs 7,500, GST drag shrinks; all future supply under Aurika sidesteps it entirely.
- "Better to have 100 individuals booking you than 1 company giving 100 room nights" — strategic push to distributed/retail demand as a resilience moat (target 65% retail at scale).
- One fully-renovated Keys hotel (Slide 56) doing Rs 11 lakh EBITDA/room; conservative target ~Rs 60 cr EBITDA from ~930 Keys rooms (<Rs 6 lakh/room); Keys RevPAR targeted toward Red Fox levels (~Rs 5,400–5,500 ARR).
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious

bull_bear.body:
- Deleveraging: "Our gross debt as on 30th June 2026 stood at Rs 1,475 crores, down 11% from Rs 1,657.9 crores a year ago and our cost of debt reduced to 7.48%, down 53 basis points versus a year ago."
- The restructuring separates the funding models: "Fleur funds asset ownership and development with a new equity line from Warburg, while Lemon Tree operates as an asset-light business"; Fleur's growth capital is "Rs 960 Cr (Warburg Pincus Primary Investment) + Strong Internal Accruals + Debt Financing Capacity".
- The asset-light entity is described as needing "minimal capital required for growth" with "70%+ steady state EBITDA margins" on fee income, and "Capital-light model enables scalable growth with minimal additional funding requirements".
- Value-accretion claim for shareholders: "Effective ownership in Fleur increases from 45.8% to 57.5%; Total Attributable EBITDA increases by 8%+ post-scheme" (Rs 402 Cr pre-scheme to Rs 434 Cr post-scheme, on FY26 figures).
- Fee income economics on the listed side: Management/Franchise fees from 3rd-party owned hotels Rs 22.8 Cr in Q1 FY27 (up 42% YoY), fees from Fleur Hotels Rs 22.6 Cr (up 6%), total management fees Rs 45.4 Cr (up 21%). No dividend or buyback policy is stated anywhere in the deck.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Scale and brand leadership in the mid-market: India's largest mid-to-upscale hotel chain with ~6% of total branded inventory and a self-described segment disruptor position in the mid-market
- Distinct multi-brand portfolio spanning economy to upscale (Aurika, Lemon Tree Premier, Keys Prima, Lemon Tree Hotels, Keys Select, Red Fox, Keys Lite), allowing the right product to be matched to guest, location and occasion
- Presence across the entire hospitality value chain — ownership, leasing, management and franchising
- Capital-efficient asset-light model: over 75% of properties managed or franchised, ~16,000 rooms in the managed/franchised portfolio
- Network effect from 268 operational and upcoming hotels across 160+ cities in India and three international markets, where growth in new cities fuels demand in existing markets
- Owned network as a strategic asset: 41 operational owned hotels with 5,759 rooms that, once stabilised, deliver high returns and can be monetised by diluting ownership while retaining majority shareholding
- Industry-leading profitability and cost structure — 48.14% EBITDA, best-in-class cost and manpower ratios, real-time cost-control towers
- Digital and revenue-management capability — bionic pricing, data-driven next-generation sales recommendations and a scalable technology stack
- Loyalty and direct-demand engine — Infinity Rewards with 23,71,923 loyalty programme members and 41.51% of rooms per day booked through the brand website and online travel agents
- Intellectual property: 173 trademarks registered
- ESG positioning — all 41 owned/leased hotels IGBC green-certified, 39.38% renewable share of electricity and 35.74% reduction in GHG emissions intensity over the FY19 baseline
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Regulatory compliance across a rapidly growing hotel network — Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as a Risk with negative financial implications: 'Deviation from a compliance is possible in a growing network'. Mitigated through an internal audit system and compliance software (Legatrix) that monitors all compliances for all hotels.
- Ethics and transparency lapses as the network scales — Flagged as a Risk with negative financial implications — 'Deviation from ethical/transparent practices is possible in a growing network'. Controls include a dual/multiple sign-off process especially for big-ticket items, an active whistle-blower policy and a strong ombudsman policy and handling mechanism.
- Data privacy and cyber breach of the loyalty database — Flagged as a Risk with negative financial implications, driven by a growing loyalty consumer database at Lemon Tree combined with innovation in hacking and breaching of data protection systems. A data privacy policy following global and Indian standards was defined in FY22 in consultation with a Big 4 firm.
- Water scarcity and water management — Flagged as a Risk with negative financial implications — water is a 'precious resource with scarcity in every destination that Lemon Tree is present in'. Mitigation is water-efficiency initiatives, recycling and reuse of all water used in the hotel, and rainwater harvesting.
- Climate change and the sector's carbon intensity — Flagged as a Risk in the BRSR material-issues table, on the rationale that the hospitality industry inherently has a high carbon footprint. (The disclosure is truncated in the source bundle mid-sentence, so the stated mitigation and financial implication could not be read.)
- Occupational health, safety, fire and food safety across hotels and construction sites — Managed through an OHS Management System covering all employees, routine and non-routine hazard identification, an Incident Tracking System, documented emergency response plans, regular safety audits, fire detection and suppression equipment across all hotels, a Food Production Manual and trained security. The company targets zero occupational health incidents across employees, contractors, guests, communities and the public; FY26 reported zero recordable work-related injuries and zero health and safety incidents at under-construction sites, with health and safety training reaching 47.23% of full-time employees.
- Human rights and labour conduct in the extended value chain and at construction sites — The Human Rights Policy, aligned to the UDHR and the ILO Declaration, sets expectations for employees, business partners and third-party contractors, with zero tolerance for sexual harassment, discrimination, child labour, forced labour and exploitation. Construction sites are monitored for violations, misconduct and unfair treatment, and all reported violations are referred to the Vigilance Officer.
- Single-activity business concentration in hotels — The Board's Report states the Company is engaged in the hotel business with no change in the nature of its business during the year, so group earnings depend on a single industry and on the performance of the 131 operational hotels and the 137-hotel development pipeline; the BRSR nonetheless cites Economic Performance as an Opportunity on the view that the business model supports stability and growth of revenues through both peaks and troughs of the business cycle.
- Board-level risk oversight is the primary control layer — The Company has a Risk Management Policy identifying elements of risk that in the Board's opinion may threaten the existence of the Company, with risk management embedded in critical business activities, functions and processes and risks reviewed for changes in nature and extent. A Risk Management Committee is one of the five mandatory Board committees, alongside the Audit, Nomination and Remuneration, CSR and Stakeholders' Relationship Committees.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body:
- **Owned/leased (→ Fleur):** Post-scheme Fleur = 5,600 rooms / 39 operational hotels, "India's largest hotel platform by inventory"; economics concentrated in top 6 cities (high barriers to entry).
- **Managed & franchised (asset-light, stays with Lemon Tree):** 3rd-party mgmt fee Rs 73.9 cr (+23% — includes new net additions/scale); Fleur mgmt fee Rs 95.8 cr (+8% — same-store, hit by GST + accelerated Fleur renovation depressing incentive fees, which scale 1%→5% of revenue by GOP/EBITDA slab).
- **Geographies:** Hotels densest in North & West; expansion runway in South, East Coast (Bengal & beyond) as they "go deeper into India." Aurika = 2 hotels (Mumbai, Udaipur); Keys spread Ludhiana–Visakhapatnam–Bangalore–Trivandrum–Cochin–Pune.
business.title: Segment (owned/managed/geographies)

business.body:
- ✅ **Lemon Tree (asset-light NewCo)** — beneficiary of demerger value-unlock, debt-free high-ROCE fee model, GST-insulated Aurika supply.
- ✅ **Fleur Hotels** — Warburg-backed largest-by-inventory owner platform with ~Rs 3,000 cr deployable firepower.
- ⭐ Aurika (highest-ARR/margin brand) and fully-renovated Keys portfolio as forward margin/RevPAR drivers.
- (Sector read-through: mid-market branded operators benefit from demand>supply structural gap and 2.5 mn unbranded rooms convertible to brands.)

business.title: Challenges → Beneficiaries

business.body:
- Claims to be the "Largest mid to upscale hotel chain with ~6% of the total branded inventory in India and segment disruptor in mid market segment", operating seven brands: Aurika Hotels & Resorts, Lemon Tree Premier, Lemon Tree Hotels, Red Fox, Keys Prima, Keys Select and Keys Lite.
- Addressable-market framing: "2.5 Mn Total Rooms in India" of which "~200K (~8%) Branded Rooms", giving "a compelling asset-light growth opportunity to tap India's ~2.3 Mn unbranded hospitality rooms"; segment split shown as Luxury/Upper Upscale 68K, Mid-scale/Economy 55K, Upscale 43K, Upper Mid-scale 34K.
- Moat asserted through distribution: "Infinity Rewards: Industry-leading loyalty program with 2.0+ Mn members", "Active Revenue Management", a sales network "on-site in 131 hotels and off-site in 8 regional offices", and proprietary platform "Totally Foxed Solutions (TFS)" driving "Lemon Tree's 2.0" digital transformation with AI/ML.
- Occupancy premium claimed versus industry (same-store): India 66% / 67% / 68% versus Lemon Tree 68% / 70% / 72% for FY2023 / FY2024 / FY2025, i.e. "+2% / +3% / +4%".
- Post-scheme Fleur is positioned as "India's Largest Hotel Platform in the mid-market segment with 39 operating hotels / 5.6k operating rooms" and shown with the highest operational rooms versus Juniper 2,133, Ventive 2,199, Chalet 3,389, SAMHI 4,899 and Fleur 5,556.
business.title: Positioning (investor deck)

business.body:
- [Demerger] A "Composite Scheme of Arrangement" with appointed date 1 April 2026: (1) "Purchase of APG's ~41% stake in Fleur by Warburg Pincus", (2) "Lemon Tree to transfer 17 hotels along with development capabilities; Fleur will issue new shares to Lemon Tree & its shareholders in exchange for these" (15 operational + 2 under-construction), (3) "Listing of Fleur as an independent entity post-Scheme" on NSE/BSE.
- [Scheme timeline] CCI approval completed April 2026 (announcement Jan 2026); pending are exchange/SEBI filing, NCLT filing with shareholder and creditor approval, and Fleur listing in CY27; the process is marked "12-15 Months" and requires "approvals from shareholders, creditors, stock exchanges, SEBI, NCLT, CCI and other regulatory authorities".
- [Post-scheme structure] Lemon Tree Hotels: Promoter Group 77.7% / Public 22.3%, revenue Rs 247 Cr and EBITDA Rs 149 Cr (FY26 pro-forma); Fleur Hotels: Warburg Pincus 41.0%, revenue Rs 1,333 Cr and EBITDA Rs 554 Cr (FY26 pro-forma), versus the current group structure of Rs 1,453 Cr consolidated revenue and Rs 699 Cr consolidated EBITDA (FY26 pre-demerger).
- [Leadership transition] "Patanjali Govind Keswani: Executive Chair at Lemon Tree until March 2027 transitioning to Non-Executive Chair after March 2027" while anchoring Fleur as Executive Chairman; Lemon Tree MD Neelendra Singh joined Oct 2025 (earlier India MD at Adidas) with Kapil Sharma as Executive Director and CFO; Fleur MD and CEO Saurabh Shatdal joined Aug 2025 (earlier MD at Cushman & Wakefield) with Mayank Sharma as CFO.
- [Related-party arrangement] Post-scheme "No exclusivity among the platforms", but "Fleur is the exclusive development partner for any owned-hotel opportunities originating within the Lemon Tree Group", and Lemon Tree retains a "~41% ownership stake" in Fleur plus a "Long-term management agreement with Fleur".
business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: Lemon Tree Hotels Limited operates and develops hotels across the economy, midscale, upper-midscale and upscale segments in India and three international markets, serving business and leisure travellers, families, tourists, event and wedding guests, F&B patrons and long-stay guests. The company is present across the hospitality value chain — ownership, leasing, management and franchising — with 131 operational hotels and 11,811 rooms as on 31 March 2026, of which 41 are owned/leased (5,759 rooms) and 90 are managed and franchised. Revenue is almost entirely from hotel services (accommodation/rooms, dining, bar, banquets, conference and meeting rooms, spa, fitness centre, swimming pool), which accounted for 98.16% of turnover.

outlook.body:
- **RevPAR/ARR strategy:** Pivot (since mid-March) to defend **occupancy at a premium to market** rather than push rate while war-driven demand is soft; rate held ~flat / maintain YoY price levels. Long-run 7–8% annual price hikes assumed.
- **Room additions / signings:** Signed 55 managed+franchised hotels / 4,912 rooms in FY26; opened 20 hotels / 1,523 rooms. Run-rate: sign ~55+ hotels/yr, open ~25 hotels/yr, with ~3-year sign-to-open lag. Openings guided ~2,000 rooms in FY27, ~3,000 FY28, ~4,000 FY29 (will reach ~5,000/yr as today's signings mature). FY27/28 ~4,500 Keys to open.
- **Margins:** GST+tech+renovation cost basket 5.8% (FY26) → 4.8% (FY27) → 3.7% (FY28 onward) = ~1% revenue saving/yr → corresponding EBITDA margin expansion. GST impact rises 1%→2% of revenue in FY27 (full year) then declines as <Rs 7,500 ARR guests shrink; stabilizes ~1.7%. Tech ~0.6–0.7% steady. Renovation normalizes to ~1.1–1.3% (vs 1.9% FY27).
- **Net debt:** Comfortable up to 4x Debt/EBITDA theoretically but stays conservative (~2.25x now). On full 2,500-room Fleur deployment (~Rs 1,500 cr capital), consolidated Fleur debt could rise temporarily to mid Rs 2,500–3,000 cr until EBITDA flows.
- **Lemon Tree (post-demerger) margins:** Currently 60% pro-forma EBITDA flow-through → target 70%+ steady state, eventually 75–80% EBITDA → ~60% PAT (no debt, no depreciation; tax 22–25%). Track over next ~2.5 years.

- **Combined operational + signed pipeline:** 22,581 rooms across 268 hotels; **operational = 11,811 rooms / 131 hotels.**
- **Asset-light (FY26):** signed 55 hotels / 4,912 rooms; opened 20 hotels / 1,523 rooms.
- **Fleur confirmed pipeline:** 4 hotels / 875 rooms. Aurika Nehru Place (572 rooms — to be North India's largest hotel) in final approval before construction (~Rs 700 cr capex, cash flow over 3.5 yrs, 60% in last 18 months). Aurika Naldehra, Shimla — 2 of 3 blocks opening by Q2. Aurika Varanasi — 47-room heritage on the Ganges ghat (signed Jan, license deal, high-rate potential).
- **Fleur growth optionality:** ~2,500 additional rooms under active discussion (greenfield / brownfield / operating-asset acquisition), top 6–7 cities + select leisure + international destinations where Indians travel.
outlook.title: Pipeline (keys under development)

outlook.body:
- **Demerger value-unlock:** Warburg completed APG stake purchase in Fleur. LTH transfers 17 hotels + development capability for Fleur shares → Fleur lists separately. Post-scheme LTH shareholders own ~74% of Fleur (33% direct + ~41% via LTH), vs LTH's current 59% direct stake (before Warburg primary infusion). Two financially sound entities; LTH = debt-free high-margin high-ROCE fee/brand co.
- **Asset-light fee compounding:** FY23–FY26 managed-portfolio fee income grew ~27%/yr; expected to grow faster as base scales. Stable hotel fees rise 50–60% once a hotel matures (first 12–18 months subdued).
- **Aurika** = highest ARR and margin brand; elevates group profile (all future supply planned under Aurika — largely unaffected by GST change).
- **Loyalty/digital optionality:** 24 lakh loyalty members; ~48–50% of room nights from loyalty guests; loyalty sign-ups drive ~25% of annual room-night volume. Next 2 years: invest in PMS, booking engine, loyalty engine, app to shift mix toward direct/retail. Target 65% retail business at 20,000–25,000 rooms.
outlook.title: Growth / Optionality

outlook.body:
- Lemon Tree 2.0 — the framework defining how the company plans to grow from here, combining asset-light expansion, digital transformation and a sharper focus on sustainability to improve guest experience, strengthen operating performance and create long-term value.
- Six strategic levers under Lemon Tree 2.0: asset-light growth and network effect, retail acceleration, efficient cost structure, digital transformation, loyalty expansion and capital recycling.
- Five focus areas: superior financial performance, mid-market hotel leadership, a strong balance sheet, leadership in digital and leadership in ESG.
- Strategic demerger announced in FY 2025-26 to create two focused businesses: Lemon Tree Hotels transitions into a debt-free, asset-light brand management and loyalty platform, while Fleur Hotels, backed by Warburg Pincus, operates as a separate asset ownership and development platform — designed to support faster portfolio growth while limiting additional capital on Lemon Tree Hotels' balance sheet and converting a larger share of growth into recurring, fee-based revenue.
- Expansion weighted towards non-metro markets — Tier II, Tier III and emerging urban centres — using the multi-brand portfolio to match each hotel to the demand profile of its location.
- Grow the managed and franchised (asset-light) portfolio, which now accounts for more than 6,000 keys, representing over half of the 11,800+ operating rooms.
- Expand across religious, cultural and heritage destinations — Rishikesh, Haridwar, Katra, Mukteshwar, Somnath, Tirupati, Dwarka, Agra, Aurangabad, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Jaipur, Udaipur, Kumbhalgarh, Jhansi and Lucknow — to build a portfolio balanced across business, leisure and pilgrimage travel.
- Build out the upscale Aurika Hotels & Resorts brand (Aurika Udaipur, Aurika Mumbai Skycity) to strengthen the premium leisure and urban hospitality position and lift room rates.
- Add column-free banquet spaces and open lawns across relevant properties to serve larger events and expand in the domestic weddings and celebrations market.
- Embed wellness into the stay rather than as a standalone amenity — Araya Spa at Aurika, Fresco Spa at Lemon Tree Premier and Lemon Tree Hotels, The Spa at Keys Prima, and Aura, the yoga studio at Lemon Tree Premier, Rishikesh.
- Build meeting and event infrastructure across the portfolio, including in Tier II and Tier III business centres, to serve MICE, entertainment and event tourism demand and balance the weekly demand mix.
- Deepen sustainability in operations — rooftop solar, open access agreements and green power purchases, water treatment and recycling, high-performance HVAC and energy-efficient building technologies, and IGBC green certification of the owned/leased estate.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Lemon Tree's expansion is increasingly asset-light. During FY 2025-26 the Company crossed the milestone of 11,000 operational rooms; as on March 31, 2026 the Group's portfolio comprised 131 operational hotels with 11,811 rooms, while the development pipeline consisted of 137 hotels with 10,770 rooms (described elsewhere in the report as an owned/leased and managed/franchised pipeline of ~11,000 rooms). During the year the Company operationalised 20 managed and franchised properties and signed 56 new hotel contracts, taking total hotel inventory to 268 hotels and 22,581 rooms across more than 160 cities and driving a 14% increase in management fee income to Rs 169.7 Crores. Management contracts and franchising now account for over 75% of the portfolio by hotel count, and this transition allowed the Company to reach its CY 2028 expansion milestone nearly two years ahead of schedule. Alongside new openings, FY26 saw a significant step-up in renovation expenditure to upgrade the owned hotel portfolio together with investments in technology; management states that nearly all future hotel-ownership supply is being planned under the upscale Aurika brand. Structurally, the Board-announced reorganisation will separate the Company into Lemon Tree Hotels — a pure-play asset-light company offering hotel management, brand and loyalty, distribution and digital services — and Fleur Hotels, a large-scale growth-oriented hotel ownership/leasing company with end-to-end in-house development capabilities, a potentially large pipeline and a significant pool of available capital, with Warburg Pincus inducted as a strategic investor and long-term capital partner for Fleur. The scheme has already achieved important regulatory milestones. The Company's growth history is milestoned as 1 hotel and 49 rooms in 2004, the IPO and 50th hotel in 2018, the Aurika brand launch and Keys Hotels acquisition in 2019, Aurika Mumbai Skycity (India's largest hotel by number of rooms) operationalised on 5 October, and 22K+ rooms across 260+ hotels and 160+ destinations as on 31 March 2026.

outlook.body:
- India's travel and tourism sector continued to expand, supported by rising domestic travel, improving connectivity and wider digital adoption, with demand growing across leisure, business, events and extended-stay travel.
- Traveller expectations shifting towards convenience, consistency, value, flexibility and personalised experiences, creating a more diverse and segmented market with opportunities across locations, formats and price points.
- Scale of the travel economy: domestic tourist visits reached approximately 4.55 billion in 2025 and total air passenger traffic exceeded 420 million, with continued investment in airports, highways and tourism infrastructure improving access.
- Hospitality demand dispersing beyond gateway cities into Tier II, Tier III and emerging urban centres; more than 64,000 hotel keys were signed in 2025 with a significant share in these markets.
- Faith-based tourism as an important domestic travel driver — the Maha Kumbh drew more than 663 million visitors — alongside growing interest in heritage, wildlife and cultural experiences.
- Experience-led travel: personalised service, wellness, local cuisine and place-rooted experiences supporting longer stays and greater willingness to spend; growth of the Aurika portfolio supported an increase in the group's Average Room Rate to Rs 6,875 in FY 2025-26 and higher total revenue per available room.
- Destination weddings and multi-day celebrations as a growing demand segment — banquets, events and weddings contribute up to 35% to 40% of total revenue at some of the larger hotels and leisure properties during peak periods.
- Wellness becoming more integral to the hospitality experience, particularly across leisure and resort destinations.
- MICE, entertainment and event tourism growing beyond the major metros on better convention infrastructure and new venues, supporting recurring corporate and institutional business.
- Sustainability increasingly shaping traveller choices, corporate procurement and investment decisions, with resource efficiency also improving operating efficiency and cost management.
- Market enablers cited as tailwinds: consumption at a tipping point, a large underserved and fragmented mid-market hotel segment, growing aspirations/affluence/willingness to spend, and demand outpacing supply.
- Post-demerger revenue mix shift towards recurring, fee-based revenue from brand management and loyalty.
- As on March 31, 2026, the development pipeline consisted of 137 hotels with 10,770 rooms, against 131 operational hotels with 11,811 rooms.
- During FY 2025-26 the company signed 56 hotels comprising 4,959 keys, with much of this pipeline located in underpenetrated regional markets.
- The portfolio reached 22,581 operational and signed pipeline rooms across 268 hotels by March 2026.
- Managed and franchised hotels now account for more than 6,000 keys, representing over half of the portfolio of 11,800+ operating rooms.

deepdive.thesis: Lemon Tree posted its best-ever FY26 across occupancy, ARR, revenue, EBITDA, PBT, PAT and cash profit, but Q4/FY26 margins compressed due to a deliberate, front-loaded "catch-up" renovation cycle, a one-time GST change, tech investment and one-off labour/property-tax items. The big structural story is the **composite demerger**: Lemon Tree becomes a pure-play, debt-free, high-ROCE asset-light management/brand/loyalty company (targeting 75–80% EBITDA / ~60% PAT margins steady state), while **Fleur Hotels** (post Warburg Pincus buying out APG) lists separately as India's largest hotel ownership platform by inventory (5,600 rooms, 39 hotels) with ~Rs 3,000 cr deployable firepower over 12–18 months for ~2,500 additional rooms. Near-term, demand is being dented by the US–Iran war and IndiGo capacity/aviation disruptions (March/April), with management pivoting to defend **occupancy over rate**.

risks.note: Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as a Risk with negative financial implications: 'Deviation from a compliance is possible in a growing network'. Mitigated through an internal audit system and compliance software (Legatrix) that monitors all compliances for all hotels.
risks.risk: Regulatory compliance across a rapidly growing hotel network

risks.note: Flagged as a Risk with negative financial implications — 'Deviation from ethical/transparent practices is possible in a growing network'. Controls include a dual/multiple sign-off process especially for big-ticket items, an active whistle-blower policy and a strong ombudsman policy and handling mechanism.
risks.risk: Ethics and transparency lapses as the network scales

risks.note: Flagged as a Risk with negative financial implications, driven by a growing loyalty consumer database at Lemon Tree combined with innovation in hacking and breaching of data protection systems. A data privacy policy following global and Indian standards was defined in FY22 in consultation with a Big 4 firm.
risks.risk: Data privacy and cyber breach of the loyalty database

risks.note: Flagged as a Risk with negative financial implications — water is a 'precious resource with scarcity in every destination that Lemon Tree is present in'. Mitigation is water-efficiency initiatives, recycling and reuse of all water used in the hotel, and rainwater harvesting.

risks.note: Managed through an OHS Management System covering all employees, routine and non-routine hazard identification, an Incident Tracking System, documented emergency response plans, regular safety audits, fire detection and suppression equipment across all hotels, a Food Production Manual and trained security. The company targets zero occupational health incidents across employees, contractors, guests, communities and the public; FY26 reported zero recordable work-related injuries and zero health and safety incidents at under-construction sites, with health and safety training reaching 47.23% of full-time employees.
risks.risk: Occupational health, safety, fire and food safety across hotels and construction sites

risks.note: The Human Rights Policy, aligned to the UDHR and the ILO Declaration, sets expectations for employees, business partners and third-party contractors, with zero tolerance for sexual harassment, discrimination, child labour, forced labour and exploitation. Construction sites are monitored for violations, misconduct and unfair treatment, and all reported violations are referred to the Vigilance Officer.
risks.risk: Human rights and labour conduct in the extended value chain and at construction sites

risks.note: The Board's Report states the Company is engaged in the hotel business with no change in the nature of its business during the year, so group earnings depend on a single industry and on the performance of the 131 operational hotels and the 137-hotel development pipeline; the BRSR nonetheless cites Economic Performance as an Opportunity on the view that the business model supports stability and growth of revenues through both peaks and troughs of the business cycle.
